Introduction:
Household-based studies are often used to identify risk factors for tuberculosis (TB) infection transmission and evaluate the efficacy of TB preventive therapies. Typically, these studies define the earliest diagnosed TB patient within a household as the index patient and subsequently monitor their household contacts (HHCs) for incident TB disease. This design assumes that HHCs who develop TB disease are likely to have been infected by their respective index patients. However, this assumption may be challenged, as some HHCs likely acquire TB infections from community sources, introducing the non-differential misclassification of TB outcomes [ 1–5 ].

In principle, such non-differential misclassification biases study results toward the null, underestimating the true magnitude of the associations. Nevertheless, when unexpected or strong associations emerge, questions regarding the robustness and validity of the findings frequently arise. These concerns become particularly important in high-TB-burden settings, in which higher levels of community-based TB exposure may increase the potential for misclassification, thus weakening the conclusions derived from household-based studies [ 6 , 7 ].

To better understand the impact of community-acquired TB infections on household-based transmission studies, it is necessary to quantify the proportion of genetically linked index–HHC pairs, as these are likely the result of within-household transmission. In this study, we address this question in two ways. First, we assess the proportion of index–HHC patient pairs that are genetically linked by using data from a longitudinal household study that we previously conducted in Lima, Peru. We then incorporate the findings from this study into a systematic review of other studies that have applied molecular genotyping methods to index–HHC patient pairs. By synthesizing evidence across diverse epidemiological contexts and combining it with our primary data, we aim to rigorously evaluate the robustness and validity of household-based study designs across settings with different TB burdens. By clarifying the extent to which household transmission can be distinguished from community-acquired infection, this work also informs the design and interpretation of contact investigations, preventive therapy trials, and vaccine studies across settings with different TB burdens.
Methods: Lima household-based cohort stu:
### Study setting and design

We conducted a prospective cohort study in 20 districts of Lima, Peru (population ∼3.3 million). The study design and methodology have been described previously [ 5 ]. Between September 2009 and August 2012, we enrolled incident pulmonary TB patients aged ≥16 years from 106 health centers and confirmed diagnoses by using sputum smear and culture. At enrolment, we collected sociodemographic and clinical data by using a structured questionnaire. Within 2 weeks of an index diagnosis, we invited HHCs to participate; consenting HHCs underwent TB symptom screening and, if positive, were referred for further evaluation. HHCs without TB at baseline were followed for 1 year, with visits at 2, 6, and 12 months. We classified HHCs diagnosed within 14 days as co-prevalent patients and those diagnosed between 14 and 455 days as secondary TB patients. Sputum samples were obtained whenever possible at enrolment or follow-up.

### Genotyping, whole-genome sequencing, and genetic distance analysis

Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( Mtb ) isolates from culture-positive index and HHC patients were genotyped by using 24-locus mycobacterial interspersed repetitive unit–variable number tandem repeat (MIRU–VNTR) typing and sequenced by using whole-genome sequencing (WGS) on the Illumina HiSeq platform. The read lengths ranged from 100 to 150 base pairs, with a minimum coverage of 20-fold. Raw WGS reads were mapped to the Mtb H37Rv reference genome by using the BWA-MEM algorithm [ 8 ]. We identified variants, including single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), by using an alignment-based approach [ 9 , 10 ]. Isolates with <95% genome mapping coverage were excluded. We considered nucleotide calls missing if the valid depth of coverage was <10% of the mean coverage of the isolate, the mean read-mapping quality was <10, or the alternative allele frequency was <85%. Variants within the PE/PPE gene family and previously identified high-error regions were excluded [ 11 , 12 ]. Index–HHC pairs in which at least one isolate showed evidence of mixed infection were excluded from the analysis [ 13 ].

### Assessment of within-household transmission for index–HHC patient pairs

As a proxy for within-household transmission, we estimated the proportion of index–HHC patient pairs who were genetically linked by using MIRU–VNTR genotyping and WGS genetic distance analysis. A genetically linked transmission event was defined using MIRU typing as an index–HHC pair with ≥23 matched loci out of 24. In the WGS analysis, a genetically linked transmission event was defined as a genetic distance of ≤12 SNPs between Mtb isolates from the index–HHC pair [ 14 ]. We reported the overall proportion of genetically linked pairs, then stratified by co-prevalent versus secondary HHCs. Because many household studies focus on child contacts, who are more likely than adults to be infected by the index patient, we also reported matching proportions for pairs with a child contact [ 15 ]. Finally, we evaluated the associations between index and HHC characteristics and within-household transmission among index–secondary patient pairs by using a modified Poisson generalized estimating equation to account for correlation between pairs from the same households.
Results: Lima household-based cohort stu:
Among 12 676 HHCs exposed to a microbiologically confirmed index patient, 692 (5%) developed TB, of whom 246 (36%) were confirmed by using culture.

### MIRU genotyping matching

Among the 246 culture-confirmed HHC patients, 192 (78%) were successfully genotyped by using MIRU–VNTR, with data available for 168 index–HHC pairs. Twenty-three (14%) showed mixed infection and were excluded, leaving 145 pairs. Of these, 81 [56%, 95% confidence interval (CI): 47%–64%] were genetically linked. Twenty-six of 51 (51%) index–co-prevalent pairs and 55 of 94 (59%) index–secondary pairs were genetically linked. The HHC patients of 28 pairs were children. Of these, 4/5 (80%) co-prevalent and 15/23 (65%) secondary pairs were linked.

### WGS matching

Of 190 index–HHC pairs with WGS data, 15 (5%) showed mixed infection and were excluded, leaving 175 pairs from 152 households. Overall, 109 pairs (62%) were genetically linked. Transmission was observed in 34 of 66 (52%, 95% CI: 39%–64%) index–co-prevalent pairs and 74 of 109 (68%, 95% CI: 58%–77%) index–secondary pairs, with most secondary pairs (72/74) differing by up to five SNPs. When restricting to the 33 pairs with a child HHC, we noted 5/8 (63%) index–co-prevalent pairs and 19/25 (76%) index–secondary pairs ( Supplementary Table 1 ). Secondary pairs with female contacts were more often linked than those with male contacts (79% vs 54%, P = .008), while the Mtb lineage was not associated with genetic linkage ( P = .342).
Methods: systematic review:
### Search strategy and study selection

We searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase for papers that reported Mtb genotyping results for TB patients within the same household. We searched for papers published between 1 January 2006 and 20 June 2025, reflecting the time period following the widespread adoption of standardized 12-locus MIRU–VNTR [ 16 ]. Supplementary Table 2 describes the search strategy for each database.

### Screening

We performed an initial title and abstract review, excluding papers that did not discuss the household contacts of TB patients. For qualifying studies, we searched the full-text files for keywords related to Mtb molecular typing. Publications containing one or more keywords underwent full-text evaluation by two independent reviewers and disagreements were resolved by a third reviewer. We excluded publications if they (i) did not involve original research on TB patients, (ii) did not include information on household membership, (iii) did not apply a qualifying genotyping method [spoligotyping, restriction fragment length polymorphisms (RFLPs), MIRU–VNTR, WGS] to Mtb samples, (iv) did not report Mtb genotype matching for household index–contact pairs, (v) enrolled fewer than five households, or (vi) obtained genotyping results for fewer than five index–contact pairs. We examined the reference lists of relevant systematic reviews for additional studies. A validation sample of 227 records was independently reviewed by a fourth reviewer, confirming the accuracy of the screening process.

### Data extraction

For qualifying studies, two reviewers extracted the following data: location and dates of patient enrolment, study design, eligibility criteria for index patients and contacts, procedure for identifying HHCs, definitions of household contacts, genotyping method(s), and the genotyping matching proportions for household patient pairs. We initially intended to extract individual patient data to assess the risk factors for genotype matching but this was unavailable in most studies. Instead, we extracted results based on the most stringent definition of matching of each study; when individual results were available, we calculated the proportion of identical genotypes. We reported the combined matching proportions for co-prevalent and secondary HHCs, and, when possible, separately for secondary HHCs as defined by the study authors. If the site-specific TB incidence was not reported in the publication, then we used WHO national estimates from the first year of enrolment or from 2000, whichever was later [ 17 ]. We also extracted individual-level metadata on age and gender when available.

### Quality assessment

We assessed the study quality by study design rigor and statistical robustness. Design rigor was scored (0–8) by using an eight-question framework on patient enrolment, household definitions, HHC follow-up, and genotyping completeness ( Supplementary Table 3 ). Statistical robustness was evaluated by the width of the Clopper–Pearson 95% CIs, with intervals of <40% considered robust.

### Modeling the relationship between TB incidence and the proportion of matching pairs

We modeled the relationship between TB incidence and the proportion of matching pairs by using a binomial generalized additive model with a logit link and spline term, with smoothness selected by using restricted maximum likelihood. For each incidence value, we estimated the fitted proportion and 95% CI on the probability scale.
Results: systematic review:
The study selection process is shown in Fig. 1 . Out of 5910 unique citations identified from the search, we completed a full-text review of 231 publications. Two reviewed studies from Brazil were follow-up publications from an earlier and larger genotyping study, so we reported data from the larger study [ 18 ]. Ultimately, 22 articles met all inclusion criteria [ 18–39 ].

The 22 included studies, all published in English, evaluated within-household transmission between approximately 12 000 index patients and 2800 household contacts with TB, enrolled between 1995 and 2023 ( Table 1 ). These studies were conducted in sub-Saharan Africa (South Africa, Ghana, Uganda, the Gambia, Malawi), South America (Brazil, Argentina, Peru), Central and Western Europe (Poland, Spain, the UK), Southeast Asia (Vietnam, the Philippines), the USA, and China. Two studies [ 19 , 21 ] included co-prevalent household patients only, 5 studies [ 18 , 24 , 26 , 30 , 31 ] included secondary household patients only, and 15 studies [ 20 , 22 , 23 , 25 , 27–29 , 32–39 ] included both. Four studies focused their enrolment on patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis [ 27 , 29 , 30 , 32 ]. The included studies encompassed a wide range of TB-burden settings, with community incidence rates ranging from 6.7 to 845 TB patients per 100 000 person-years. The number of index–HHC pairs with genotyping data ranged from 6 to 344 per study, with a median of 17.5 pairs ( Table 2 ). Genotyping for one or more index–child HHC pairs was available for five studies and gender information for patient pairs was partially or completely available for eight studies ( Supplementary Tables 4 and 5 ).

### Quality assessment

Among the 22 studies from the systematic review, 10 studies (45%) [ 18–21 , 24–27 , 29 , 36 ] were scored as ≥5/8 for study design. The most common methodological gaps were the failure to report the proportion of eligible index patients who agreed to participate ( Supplementary Table 3 , Question 2), the lack of active follow-up to detect incident TB among HHCs ( Supplementary Table 3 , Question 7), and the prolonged interval allowed between the index patient’s diagnosis and the subsequent diagnosis of HHC TB patients ( Supplementary Table 3 , Question 8).

Eleven (50%) reviewed studies reported matching proportions with a Clopper–Pearson exact 95% CI width of >40% [ 19–21 , 24 , 26–30 , 33 , 38 ]. Therefore, only 11 reviewed studies were considered statistically robust ( Fig. 2 ).

### Host factors and within-household transmission

Among the 11 reviewed studies that met our criteria for statistical robustness, three reported genetic linkage by age ( Supplementary Table 4 ). However, two of these studies [ 31 , 34 ] included three or fewer child contacts. In the third study [ 25 ], the matching proportion was 90% (26/29) in pairs with child contacts and 63% (20/32) in pairs with adult contacts. Three statistically robust studies reported gender information for comparison ( Supplementary Table 5 ). One study [ 37 ] reported 100% matching for all pair types and the two other studies [ 31 , 34 ] found matching proportions that were similar for female and male contacts, with slightly higher values in females (88% vs 81%, P = .656; 73% vs 70%, P = .999).
Results: proportion of within-household:
### All pairs (index–co-prevalent and index–secondary patient pairs)

Across 23 studies (22 from the review and our Lima study), the proportion of genetically matched index–HHC pairs ranged from 17% to 100%. Of six studies using multiple methods independently, five reported variability across the methods. No method universally yielded higher or lower proportions, though spoligotyping gave the highest proportions in three out of four studies. Eleven studies used MIRU–VNTR (with varying loci) and seven implemented WGS ( Table 2 ).

Among the 12 total studies with greater statistical robustness [ 18 , 22 , 23 , 25 , 31 , 32 , 34–37 , 39 ], 10 reported an overall matching proportion of ≥62% and two studies from the same cohort in Malawi reported proportions of 44% and 49%, respectively ( Fig. 2a ). The nine studies that reported a matching proportion of ≥62% were conducted in settings with a TB incidence of ≤276 patients per 100 000 person-years, while the studies from Malawi were conducted in an area with a TB burden of 386 patients per 100 000 person-years.

The spline regression model of all patient pairs suggests that, in study settings with an annual TB incidence of ≤250 per 100 000 population, at ≥61% (95% CI: 55%–67%) of household patients are genetically matched to their index patient, likely reflecting household TB infection transmission ( Fig. 2b ). However, estimates of the matching proportion in regions of exceptionally high TB incidence are limited by sparse data.

### Index–secondary patient pairs only

Eleven studies, including our study in Lima, reported a separate matching proportion for index–secondary patient pairs ( Fig. 3 ). Five studies were statistically robust, though all of these were conducted in settings of low or moderate TB incidence. Secondary matching proportions were equivalent to or higher than overall matching in all studies except for Robbins et al. , who reported a secondary matching proportion of 55% for exact spoligotype and RFLP matches. However, the inclusion of near genotype matches increases this proportion to 88%, highlighting the challenge of comparing across typing methods and definitions of concordance.
Discussion:
Here, we found that, in settings with a TB incidence of ≤250 cases per 100 000 person-years, the majority of index–HHC patient pairs are genetically matched, regardless of the genotyping method employed, suggesting that within-household transmission predominates at low to moderate TB incidence. However, substantial variation was observed in settings with higher TB burdens (>250 cases per 100 000 person-years), likely due to limited genotyping data and smaller sample sizes.

Genotyping tools differ in resolution: WGS offers the highest, RFLP and MIRU–VNTR moderate, and spoligotyping the lowest. Higher-resolution methods often yield lower matching proportions [ 40 ]. Within the same studies, the matching proportions varied, depending on the genotyping method used. Spoligotyping typically produced higher proportions, while no consistent pattern emerged with WGS, RFLP, and MIRU–VNTR. These inconsistencies may reflect the greater ability of WGS to detect mixed infections and its sensitivity to sputum quality, both of which affect matching calculations and contribute to discrepancies with RFLP and MIRU–VNTR.

Although all studies defined the earliest diagnosed TB patient in a household as the index or “source” patient, only four actively and prospectively followed HHCs to track incident TB disease. Most studies relied on national TB registries to retrospectively identify secondary patients, often diagnosed years after the index patient. In the studies from Malawi that reported matching proportions of <50%, the time between the index and contact patient diagnoses was allowed to be >10 years. This delay increases the likelihood that household cases are community-acquired rather than originating from household transmission. If these retrospective studies had limited the diagnostic interval between the index and secondary HHC patients to ≤2years, the reported matching proportions would likely have been higher. Thus, in settings with a TB incidence of ≤250 cases per 100 000 person-years, the actual proportion attributable to household transmission likely exceeds the estimated 61%.

Household contacts’ age and gender may also influence the within-household transmission dynamics. Many household-based studies, particularly clinical trials of TB preventive therapy, focus on child contacts to minimize misclassification, assuming that children have limited social interactions and are primarily infected by their index patient [ 5 , 41 , 42 ]. Our Lima study and Whalen et al. observed a trend toward higher matching proportions among pediatric contacts compared with adults, consistently with the rationale for child-contact study designs. Gender-based household roles may further shape transmission. Several systematic review studies indicate that women spend more time at home due to caregiving and domestic responsibilities [ 43–46 ], likely leading to increased exposure to infectious household members. This likely explains the higher matching proportions observed among female HHCs.

Our systematic review has limitations. First, despite a rigorous search strategy, we may have inadvertently missed relevant studies due to search-term constraints. Secondly, most included studies relied on data collected over a decade ago. Advances in diagnostics, community-based TB control, and expanded TB preventive therapy coverage may have altered the transmission dynamics, meaning that older findings may not fully reflect the current realities. Third, the limited sample size of index–HHC pairs in most studies precluded formal statistical testing; therefore, we presented descriptive analyses only, which restricts the extent to which we can draw statistical inferences. Fourth, we assumed that non-matched index–HHC pairs reflect community-acquired infection. In the absence of additional contact tracing or social network data, we cannot rule out the possibility that some of these pairs may instead represent unrecognized household transmission chains, which could lead to an overestimation of community-acquired infection.

In summary, our findings suggest that, in settings with a TB incidence of ≤250 per 100 000 person-years, 20%–40% of incident HHC TB patients may be misclassified as having had household transmission, with lower misclassification when analyses focus on child or female contacts. Its impact in high-incidence settings remains unclear. Because TB preventive therapy trials span countries with varying TB burdens, misclassification differences must be considered. Predictive modeling has been proposed to address community-acquired infections but standardized methods and validation are needed to better characterize household transmission in high-burden settings.
